summary: Describes a simple programming interface to cryptographic functions that applications can call. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A short menu of simple buttons that a programmer can press to scramble or check data, without needing to know the math behind them.

questions: how does the crypto api work
subtitle: A simple programming interface to cryptographic functions, separating crypto libraries from applications.

tldr.problem: Applications that need cryptographic functions at the operating system kernel level historically had to compile and link cryptographic libraries directly into their code, tightly coupling crypto implementation with application logic.
tldr.mechanism: The Simple Cryptographic Program Interface (Crypto API) defines a standard interface for cryptographic plugins as separate OS modules (drivers or shared libraries), with functions for initialization, context management, key verification, and data transformation. It supports encryption, decryption, signing, verification, compression, hashing, and random number generation.
tldr.outcome: Applications can call cryptographic functions through a standard interface without needing to know the details of the crypto library, enabling independent development of crypto implementations and applications.

today: RFC 2628 is an Informational document describing the Crypto API. Similar standardized cryptographic interfaces have been developed since, including the Linux Kernel Crypto API and OpenSSL's EVP interface, though this RFC represented an early effort to standardize such an interface.

sections.title: Problem and Solution
sections.content:
Internet applications requiring cryptographic functions at the operating system kernel level historically had to compile and link cryptographic libraries directly into the modules (drivers) providing application functionality. This tight coupling made it difficult to update the crypto library independently or support multiple implementations. The Simple Cryptographic Program Interface (Crypto API) addresses this by extracting cryptographic algorithms into separate, independently-developed modules.

The Crypto API defines a standard, open interface optimized for both application and kernel-level use. The interface separates the concerns of cryptographic functionality from the operating system-specific mechanisms for integrating that functionality. This enables programmers to develop applications and cryptographic modules independently while maintaining compatibility, provided both sides implement the same standard interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of building encryption right into every application, the Crypto API lets you plug in different encryption modules like LEGO blocks. Applications call the same buttons, no matter which encryption method is underneath.

sections.title: Cryptoplugin Architecture
sections.content:
A cryptoplugin is implemented as a separate operating system driver or module consisting of two parts: the cryptolibrary itself (containing the actual cryptographic algorithms) and a system-dependent wrapper that translates between the Cryptographic Program Interface and the OS-specific interface used by the plugin's client. The wrapper does not include algorithm-specific logic or client-specific functionality; it simply bridges between the two interfaces.

A cryptoplugin can contain multiple algorithms and even multiple implementations of the same algorithm with different parameters. This modular structure allows applications to discover which algorithms and implementations are available at runtime, supporting version independence between the application and the cryptographic implementation. The separation of the wrapper from the cryptolibrary means vendors can provide wrappers for different operating systems while the crypto logic remains portable.
sections.plainLanguage: A cryptoplugin has two pieces: the math part that does encryption, and a translator part that speaks to the computer. The translator lets different operating systems talk to the same math without changing it.

sections.title: Core Functions and Data Structures
sections.content:
The Crypto API defines eight main categories of functions: initialization and finalization (loading the plugin, querying available algorithms, and cleaning up), context management (opening, reopening, and closing cryptographic contexts for specific algorithm instances), key verification (checking for weak keys), data transformation (performing the actual crypto operation), and control operations.

Each algorithm is described by a CryptoAlgInfo structure containing type (encryption, decryption, signing, verification, compression, hashing, random generation), version, implementation group, maximum simultaneous contexts, and type-specific parameters. For encryption algorithms, this includes block length, key length, output length, and initialization vector size. Hash algorithms specify block length and output hash length. This metadata allows applications to query capabilities and choose appropriate algorithms for their needs.
sections.plainLanguage: The API has functions to start up the encryption module, pick which method you want, give it data to encrypt, and clean up when done. Each method tells you how big your keys and data blocks need to be.

sections.title: Supported Algorithm Types
sections.content:
The Crypto API supports seven algorithm types: encryption and decryption for symmetric ciphers, signing and verification for asymmetric cryptography, compression and decompression, hashing for one-way functions, and random number generation. For encryption, the interface supports both block ciphers (which process fixed-size blocks and require an initialization vector or ECB mode) and stream ciphers (which process arbitrary amounts of data). The transformation function is history-dependent for compression and hashing (state carries between calls) but history-independent for encryption and signing operations.

The interface allows querying a key for weakness before use, important for algorithms like DES that have known weak keys. The data transformation function is flexible: applications can pass NULL for output buffers to get the required size without performing actual transformation, supporting in-place operations or pre-allocation of output buffers.
sections.plainLanguage: The API handles many types of crypto work: scrambling data in secret (encryption), proving you wrote something (digital signatures), shrinking files (compression), creating fingerprints of data (hashing), and making random numbers. Each type has its own rules about how to use it.

sections.title: Cryptographic Context Lifecycle
sections.content:
A cryptographic context represents an instance of an algorithm with a specific key or configuration. The lifecycle begins with CryptoOpen, which initializes a context with a provided key and returns a handle. The handle is then used in subsequent transformation calls. CryptoReOpen allows changing the key without deallocating and reallocating system resources. The maximum number of simultaneously-open contexts is algorithm-dependent; stateless algorithms like hash and random generation typically support unlimited contexts (or only environmental resource limits), while stateful algorithms may have limits.

Contexts are destroyed by CryptoClose, which deallocates associated resources. The plugin tracks all open contexts and can report if contexts remain open during shutdown. Error conditions are reported through status codes: CRYPTO_OK for success, CRYPTO_ERR_NO_RESOURCES for insufficient resources (caller may retry after freeing memory), and CRYPTO_ERR_NO_MEMORY for out-of-memory conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening a context is like turning on a light switch with your secret key set. While it is on, you can transform data. Reopening lets you change your key without turning it off. Closing shuts it down and releases the memory.

sections.title: Design Objectives and Use Cases
sections.content:
The Crypto API aims to achieve several key objectives: extracting cryptographic algorithm implementations into separate, independently-developed modules; providing version independence between applications and cryptographic implementations; ensuring platform-independent development with portable source code; and enabling independent development and interoperability of separately-developed modules. These goals support use in Internet protocols such as IPsec, ISAKMP, IKE, and TLS, where the crypto layer must be decoupled from protocol logic.

The interface is designed for both user-space applications and kernel-level drivers, making it suitable for diverse deployment scenarios. By standardizing the interface while leaving OS-specific integration details to the wrapper layer, the Crypto API enables a rich ecosystem of crypto implementations that applications can use without modification, promoting adoption and security updates.
sections.plainLanguage: The Crypto API lets different people work on encryption separately from the applications that use it. A company can update their encryption without rewriting all their programs. Different operating systems can use the same encryption code.
